title: Bellarmine: the divine motion is received according to the will's negative determination (De Lib. Arb. IV.16)
source_text: XIV. Bellarminus ut difficultatem illam solvat, dicit influxum, seu Virtutem Dei, qua Voluntas movetur & applicatur ad opus, recipi in causis secundis secundum illarum dispositionem. Illa vero dispositio secundum quam recipitur in Voluntate motus Dei, Bellarmino nihil aliud est quam negativa quaedam determinatio praecedens tum influxum Dei, tum actum elicitum Voluntatis. Nimirum illa ex ejus sensu, in eo consistit quod Voluntas sinat se moveri ab objecto per rationem ipsi proposito, vel ab eo se moveri non sinat. Quam determinationem dicit esse negativam, quia non consistit in actu positivo, sed in negatione actus; cum tamen Voluntas non minus sit libera ut agat, quam ut non agat. Unde fieri putat ut Voluntas sit vere libera, & ipsa se determinet, tametsi Deus illam moveat & applicet ad opus, quia, scilicet, ipsa Dei motio in ejus potestate est. Nam, inquit, si se moveri sinat ab objecto proposito, Deus eam applicat & movet ad actum eliciendum: si non sinat, Deus eam non applicat neque movet: ad hoc, scilicet, Deus se libere obligavit, quando liberam Voluntatem creavit. De Liber. Arbitr. lib. 4. cap. 16.
pass_a_gloss: Bellarmine to solve that difficulty, says that the influence, or Power of God, by which the Will is moved and applied to the work, is received in second causes according to their disposition. But that disposition according to which the motion of God is received in the Will, is to Bellarmine nothing else than a certain negative determination preceding both the influence of God, and the elicited act of the Will. Namely that in his sense, consists in this that the Will allows itself to be moved by the object proposed to it by reason, or does not allow itself to be moved by it. Which determination he says is negative, because it does not consist in a positive act, but in the negation of an act; since yet the Will is no less free to act, than not to act. Whence he thinks it comes about that the Will is truly free, and determines itself, although God moves it and applies it to the work, because, namely, the very motion of God is in its power. For, he says, if it allows itself to be moved by the object proposed, God applies it and moves it to eliciting the act: if it does not allow, God neither applies nor moves it: to this, namely, God freely bound himself, when he created a free Will. On Free Choice book 4. chap. 16.
pass_b_english: To resolve that difficulty Bellarmine says that God's influence or power, by which the will is moved and applied to its work, is received in secondary causes according to their disposition.

For Bellarmine the disposition according to which God's motion is received in the will is simply a kind of negative determination that comes before both God's influence and the will's elicited act. In his sense it consists in the will's letting itself be moved by the object that reason sets before it, or not letting itself be moved by it. He calls the determination negative because it lies not in a positive act but in the absence of one, though the will is no less free to act than not to act.

This, he thinks, is how the will is truly free and determines itself even though God moves it and applies it to its work: God's motion itself is in the will's power. 'If it lets itself be moved by the object set before it,' he says, 'God applies it and moves it to produce the act; if it does not, God neither applies it nor moves it. God freely bound himself to this when he created a free will.' (De libero arbitrio, book 4, chapter 16.)

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.
